title: Ghee Pulling, Millet Bowls, and Turmeric Everything: How Indian Grandmothers' Wisdom Became America's Hottest Wellness Trend
excerpt: From A2 ghee in your morning coffee to makhana as the new popcorn, traditional Indian superfoods are conquering American wellness culture — and the diaspora has complicated feelings about it.
body:
Your grandmother knew. She just did not have an Instagram account.

The golden turmeric latte that Erewhon sells for $12 is the haldi doodh your nani made you drink when you had a cold. The A2 ghee that fitness influencers swear by is the same clarified butter your mother used to temper dal. The makhana that Whole Foods now stocks as a "superfood snack" is what your family ate during Navratri fasting.

In 2026, the American wellness industry has fully embraced what Indian kitchens have practised for centuries — and the diaspora is watching with a mix of pride, bemusement, and occasional exasperation.

## The Ghee Renaissance

Ghee's transformation from "that greasy Indian butter" to premium wellness product is perhaps the most dramatic. A2 ghee — made from the milk of indigenous Indian cow breeds — has become a staple in keto, paleo, and Ayurvedic wellness circles. Its high smoke point makes it a favourite among fitness enthusiasts, while its butyrate content is praised for gut health.

The trend has gone further in 2026. "Ghee pulling" — swishing a spoonful of warm ghee in the mouth for five to twenty minutes, an Ayurvedic practice called gandusha — is being recommended by nutritionists as a hack for gum health. Adding ghee to black coffee, a variation on the bulletproof coffee trend, has become routine in wellness circles. Social media fitness creators regularly feature A2 ghee in their content about clean eating and traditional nutrition.

Pure Indian Foods, a New Jersey-based company founded by Sandeep Agarwal, has ridden this wave with products like Turmeric Superghee, which concentrates curcumin in a fat-soluble form for maximum absorption — exactly the principle behind combining turmeric with ghee and black pepper in traditional Indian cooking.

## Millets and the Fibermaxxing Movement

India's International Year of Millets campaign in 2023 planted seeds that are now bearing fruit in American grocery aisles. Ragi, jowar, and bajra — gluten-free, fibre-rich staples that millions of Indians ate daily before rice and wheat took over — are being rediscovered as "ancient grains" by the Western wellness movement.

The trend aligns with what nutritionists are calling "fibermaxxing" — a focus on high-fibre foods for gut health, metabolic stability, and sustained energy. Millets fit perfectly: they are slow-digesting carbohydrates that prevent the sugar crashes associated with processed grains. Indian brands are capitalizing, with millet-based snacks, cereals, and ready-to-eat products appearing on American shelves.

## The Makhana Moment

Fox nuts, or makhana, may be 2026's breakout Indian snack in America. Long eaten during Hindu fasts and as a light evening snack in Bihar and eastern India, roasted makhana is being repositioned as a high-protein, low-calorie alternative to popcorn. Several Indian-American brands have launched flavoured makhana lines — from Himalayan salt to sriracha — targeting the health-conscious American snacker.

## The Diaspora's Dilemma

For NRIs, the mainstreaming of Indian superfoods is a double-edged sword. There is genuine pride in seeing turmeric lattes on café menus and ghee on Whole Foods shelves. But there is also the sting of cultural erasure — the quiet removal of India from "Indian food," the repackaging of ancient wisdom as a Silicon Valley biohack.

"My mom got made fun of for her tiffin box in school," one Reddit user wrote recently. "Now the same kids are paying $15 for a turmeric-ginger-black-pepper shot at a juice bar."

## What's Next

The trend shows no signs of slowing. Fermented Indian foods — curd, kanji, achaar — are being positioned as the next probiotic frontier. Amla, the Indian gooseberry, is appearing in American supplement aisles. And Ayurvedic concepts like eating seasonally and combining foods for optimal digestion are being repackaged as cutting-edge nutritional science. The knowledge was always there. The West is just finally catching up.
